Yes. In fact, the asymptotic supremum is exactly 1+o(1)1+o(1). The upper bound follows from a random divisibility-chain argument; the quoted examples with Ω(n)=k\Omega(n)=k show the constant 11 is sharp.

Let Ω(n)\Omega(n) denote the number of prime factors of nn, counted with multiplicity, and write pα∥np^\alpha\Vert n when pα∣np^\alpha\mid n but pα+1∤np^{\alpha+1}\nmid n.

The random chain

For every prime pp, let YpY_p be independent with exponential tail

P(Yp≥t)=p−t(t≥0).\mathbb P(Y_p\ge t)=p^{-t}\qquad(t\ge 0).

Equivalently, YpY_p is exponential with rate log⁡p\log p. For t>1t>1, define

N(t):=∏pp⌊Yp/t⌋.N(t):=\prod_p p^{\lfloor Y_p/t\rfloor}.

This is almost surely a finite integer for every t>1t>1, because

∑pP(Yp≥t)=∑pp−t<∞.\sum_p \mathbb P(Y_p\ge t)=\sum_p p^{-t}<\infty.

Also, if t1>t2>1t_1>t_2>1, then

⌊Yp/t1⌋≤⌊Yp/t2⌋\lfloor Y_p/t_1\rfloor\le \lfloor Y_p/t_2\rfloor

for every prime pp, so

N(t1)∣N(t2).N(t_1)\mid N(t_2).

Thus, as tt decreases from ∞\infty to 11, the values N(t)N(t) form a random divisibility chain.

For an integer n≥2n\ge 2, define

Hn:={∃ t>1:N(t)=n},H_n:=\{\exists\,t>1:N(t)=n\},

and let

h(n):=P(Hn).h(n):=\mathbb P(H_n).

If AA is primitive, then the events {Ha:a∈A}\{H_a:a\in A\} are pairwise disjoint: if a single chain hits both aa and bb, then one of a,ba,b divides the other. Hence, for every primitive set AA,

∑a∈Ah(a)≤1.\sum_{a\in A} h(a)\le 1.

So it remains to show that, uniformly for large nn,

h(n)≥(1−o(1))1nlog⁡n.h(n)\ge (1-o(1))\frac1{n\log n}.

Exact hitting probability

Let

n=∏pα∥npα.n=\prod_{p^\alpha\Vert n}p^\alpha.

The chain hits nn when, for some t>1t>1, the required prime-power thresholds have appeared but no forbidden threshold has appeared. A direct calculation gives

h(n)=∫1∞n−tζ(t)(∑pα∥nαlog⁡p1−p−t) dt.h(n) = \int_1^\infty \frac{n^{-t}}{\zeta(t)} \left( \sum_{p^\alpha\Vert n}\frac{\alpha\log p}{1-p^{-t}} \right)\,dt.

Here is the derivation. Suppose the last required threshold is the α\alpha-th threshold of a prime pα∥np^\alpha\Vert n, occurring at parameter tt. Then Yp=αtY_p=\alpha t, with density

αlog⁡p⋅p−αt dt.\alpha\log p\cdot p^{-\alpha t}\,dt.

For every other qβ∥nq^\beta\Vert n, we need

βt<Yq<(β+1)t,\beta t<Y_q<(\beta+1)t,

which has probability

q−βt(1−q−t).q^{-\beta t}(1-q^{-t}).

For every prime r∤nr\nmid n, we need Yr<tY_r<t, which has probability 1−r−t1-r^{-t}. Multiplying and summing over the possible final primes gives

h(n)=∑pα∥n∫1∞αlog⁡p⋅p−αt∏qβ∥nq≠pq−βt(1−q−t)∏r∤n(1−r−t) dt=∫1∞n−tζ(t)(∑pα∥nαlog⁡p1−p−t) dt.\begin{aligned} h(n) &= \sum_{p^\alpha\Vert n} \int_1^\infty \alpha\log p\cdot p^{-\alpha t} \prod_{\substack{q^\beta\Vert n\\q\ne p}} q^{-\beta t}(1-q^{-t}) \prod_{r\nmid n}(1-r^{-t})\,dt \\ &= \int_1^\infty \frac{n^{-t}}{\zeta(t)} \left( \sum_{p^\alpha\Vert n}\frac{\alpha\log p}{1-p^{-t}} \right)\,dt. \end{aligned}

Now observe that for t>1t>1,

∑pα∥nαlog⁡p1−p−t≥∑pα∥nαlog⁡p=log⁡n.\sum_{p^\alpha\Vert n}\frac{\alpha\log p}{1-p^{-t}} \ge \sum_{p^\alpha\Vert n}\alpha\log p = \log n.

Therefore

h(n)≥(log⁡n)∫1∞n−tζ(t) dt.h(n) \ge (\log n)\int_1^\infty \frac{n^{-t}}{\zeta(t)}\,dt.

Let L=log⁡nL=\log n. Restricting the integral to 1<t<1+δ1<t<1+\delta, with δ>0\delta>0, and writing t=1+σt=1+\sigma, we get

h(n)≥Ln−1∫0δe−Lσζ(1+σ) dσ.h(n) \ge L n^{-1}\int_0^\delta \frac{e^{-L\sigma}}{\zeta(1+\sigma)}\,d\sigma.

Since

ζ(1+σ)=1σ+O(1)(σ↓0),\zeta(1+\sigma)=\frac1\sigma+O(1) \qquad(\sigma\downarrow 0),

we have, uniformly for 0<σ≤δ0<\sigma\le\delta,

1ζ(1+σ)≥(1−η(δ))σ,\frac1{\zeta(1+\sigma)}\ge (1-\eta(\delta))\sigma,

where η(δ)→0\eta(\delta)\to 0 as δ→0\delta\to 0. Hence

h(n)≥(1−η(δ))Ln−1∫0δe−Lσσ dσ=(1−η(δ))1nL(1−e−δL(1+δL)).\begin{aligned} h(n) &\ge (1-\eta(\delta))L n^{-1} \int_0^\delta e^{-L\sigma}\sigma\,d\sigma \\ &= (1-\eta(\delta))\frac1{nL} \left(1-e^{-\delta L}(1+\delta L)\right). \end{aligned}

Choose, for example,

δ=δx:=(log⁡x)−1/2.\delta=\delta_x:=(\log x)^{-1/2}.

Then for every n≥xn\ge x, L=log⁡n≥log⁡xL=\log n\ge \log x, so

e−δxL(1+δxL)≤e−log⁡x(1+log⁡x)=o(1),e^{-\delta_x L}(1+\delta_x L) \le e^{-\sqrt{\log x}}\bigl(1+\sqrt{\log x}\bigr) =o(1),

and also η(δx)=o(1)\eta(\delta_x)=o(1). Thus, uniformly for all n≥xn\ge x,

h(n)≥(1−o(1))1nlog⁡n.h(n)\ge (1-o(1))\frac1{n\log n}.

Applying the chain to a primitive set

Let A⊂[x,∞)A\subset[x,\infty) be primitive. For every finite B⊂AB\subset A, the disjointness of the hitting events gives

∑b∈Bh(b)≤1.\sum_{b\in B}h(b)\le 1.

Using the uniform lower bound for h(b)h(b), we obtain

(1−o(1))∑b∈B1blog⁡b≤∑b∈Bh(b)≤1.(1-o(1))\sum_{b\in B}\frac1{b\log b} \le \sum_{b\in B}h(b) \le 1.

Therefore

∑b∈B1blog⁡b≤1+o(1),\sum_{b\in B}\frac1{b\log b}\le 1+o(1),

with the o(1)o(1) depending only on xx, not on BB or AA. Taking the supremum over finite B⊂AB\subset A gives

∑a∈A1alog⁡a≤1+o(1).\sum_{a\in A}\frac1{a\log a}\le 1+o(1).

So the proposed assertion is true.

Moreover, the constant 11 is best possible: for Ak={n:Ω(n)=k}A_k=\{n:\Omega(n)=k\}, one has Ak⊂[2k,∞)A_k\subset[2^k,\infty), AkA_k is primitive, and your quoted asymptotic gives

∑Ω(n)=k1nlog⁡n=1−(c+o(1))k22−k.\sum_{\Omega(n)=k}\frac1{n\log n} = 1-(c+o(1))k^2 2^{-k}.

Thus the asymptotic upper bound 1+o(1)1+o(1) cannot be replaced by anything below 11.
